description: Financial revolution, Mughal trade and the establishment of Britain's commercial empire.
content_html:
The Financial Revolution

The wars of William III against Louis XIV of France were hugely expensive. England could not fund them from taxation alone. The solution was a financial revolution that transformed how the English state raised money. In 1694, a group of London merchants led by William Paterson agreed to lend the government £1.2 million in exchange for the right to incorporate as the Bank of England. This was not just a bank — it was the foundation of a system of public credit that allowed England to borrow far more than any absolute monarchy could. By 1714, the national debt stood at around £54 million, but England had won its wars.

Key Fact

The Bank of England was founded in 1694. The initial loan of £1.2 million to the government funded war against France. By underpinning the national debt with parliamentary guarantee, it allowed England to borrow at lower interest rates than France, giving the English state a decisive financial advantage in prolonged warfare.

The East India Company and Trade with Asia

The East India Company (EIC) had been trading with Asia since 1600, but its position grew dramatically in the late seventeenth century. In 1698, the Company established a factory (trading post) at Kolkata (Calcutta). The EIC obtained trading rights through negotiation with the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb and local nawabs (governors). It is important to note that in this period the Company operated as a guest of Mughal political authority, not as a colonial ruler — the Mughal Empire remained a formidable power and the EIC depended on its goodwill for access.

Trade with India brought enormous wealth to England: Indian textiles (calicoes, muslins, silks), spices, indigo and saltpetre flowed west, while English woolens and silver went east. Indian cotton textiles were so popular in England that English wool weavers petitioned Parliament against them. The Calico Acts (1690 and 1720) attempted to restrict Indian textile imports to protect English manufacturers. Trade with Asia also helped fund the growing consumer culture in England — the middle classes could now buy exotic goods that had previously been the preserve of royalty.

Joint-stock companies like the EIC allowed investors to pool capital and share risk. This was a relatively new financial mechanism that enabled trade ventures too large and expensive for any individual merchant. Investors bought “stocks” (shares) and received dividends from profits. The EIC held a royal monopoly on English trade with Asia; its monopoly was renewed by Parliament in 1700. By 1710 its stock was among the most valuable in London.

Trade with China and the Growth of New Habits

The EIC also ran a significant trade with China through Canton (Guangzhou), importing tea, silk and porcelain. Tea was transforming English society: by the early eighteenth century it had moved from an aristocratic luxury to a middle-class staple. By c.1720 the EIC was importing millions of pounds of tea per year. The ritual of tea-drinking reshaped domestic culture, created demand for ceramic teapots and cups, and required sugar — linking the Asian trade to the Atlantic slave economy. Coffee from the Middle East, chocolate from the Americas, and tobacco from Virginia all followed similar routes from imperial trade to everyday English habit.

Key Fact

England’s commercial advantage rested on three interlocking innovations: the Bank of England (1694) enabling cheap state borrowing; the East India Company (1600, expanded 1698–1700) controlling Asian trade; and joint-stock investment spreading risk across many investors, making large-scale ventures possible.

The Treaty of Methuen (1703) between England and Portugal gave English woollen goods preferential access to Portuguese markets in exchange for similar treatment for Portuguese wine in England. This diverted English wine consumption from France (an enemy) to Portugal (an ally), and opened Portugal’s Brazilian trade routes to English merchants. Port wine became fashionable in England partly as a result of this strategic trade deal. It shows how war with France shaped commercial choices throughout the period.

Economic Impact on English Society

The financial and commercial revolution of the 1690s did not benefit all English people equally. The London merchant class and the landed gentry who invested in joint-stock companies grew wealthier. Small traders and craftspeople who lacked capital could not participate in the new financial instruments. The national debt meant the government paid interest to wealthy bondholders, funded by taxes that fell on ordinary consumers. Critics of the new financial order — including the writers Jonathan Swift and Daniel Defoe — warned that “moneyed men” were displacing the traditional landed gentry and corrupting political life. Defoe wrote extensively about commerce and trade, but also satirised the speculative mania of the early eighteenth century.

The growth of the national debt and the Bank of England’s credit system were also tied to England’s wars. William III’s Nine Years’ War (1689–1697) and the subsequent War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1713) were funded largely through borrowing. John Churchill, Duke of Marlborough, commanded English and allied forces in campaigns across Europe — Blenheim (1704), Ramillies (1706), Oudenarde (1708) — at enormous cost. The Bank of England’s ability to raise money made these campaigns possible and gave England a decisive military-financial advantage over France, whose state finances collapsed under the strain of the same wars. Empire and warfare were thus closely connected: trade profits funded armies, and armies extended the reach of trade.
exam_tip_html: For a question about the economic impact of empire, link the Bank of England (state credit), the East India Company (Asian trade), and the consumer revolution (tea, textiles, sugar) as a connected system rather than separate topics. Examiners reward answers that show how these developments reinforced each other. Avoid describing the EIC as a colonial ruler of India in this period — it operated under Mughal permission and was primarily a trading concern, not a governing body, before the mid-eighteenth century.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Bank of England (1694), founded with an initial loan of £1.2 million, created a system of public credit backed by Parliament, allowing England to borrow cheaply and fund prolonged wars against France.
  • The East India Company established a trading post at Kolkata in 1698, operating with Mughal permission; it traded Indian textiles, tea and spices, transforming English consumer habits and generating vast commercial wealth.
  • Joint-stock investment spread financial risk across shareholders, enabling large-scale trade ventures; England’s commercial system of bank credit, joint-stock companies and Asian trade gave it structural advantages over rival powers.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Bank of England when it was founded in 1694.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. it made an initial loan of Â£1.2 million to the government, which in return granted the right to incorporate as a bank and issue notes). Secure: Correct feature with some supporting information. Developing: Vague reference without specific detail. Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the East India Company's trade in this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. established a factory at Kolkata in 1698; imported Indian textiles that were so popular they threatened English wool weavers) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the founding of the Bank of England in 1694 was significant for England's military and commercial power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking the Bank of England to cheap borrowing, national debt, funding of war against France, and long-term commercial advantage with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one consequence explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the East India Company for the growth of Britain's commercial empire in the period 1688â€“c.1730? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument evaluating EIC's role (Asian trade, Kolkata, consumer revolution) alongside other commercial developments (Bank of England, Atlantic trade), with judgement on relative significance and counter-argument (e.g. EIC's position in India was still dependent on Mughal goodwill). Secure: Clear argument with evidence across more than one dimension. Developing: Some argument; may focus on only one aspect. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why English merchants and the government saw the East India Company's trade as essential for national wealth.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation showing the volume of Asian trade, the goods imported (textiles, tea, spices), the employment of joint-stock investment, and the generation of customs revenue, with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of joint-stock companies in this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. shareholders pooled capital and shared risk; the EIC held a royal monopoly renewed by Parliament in 1700) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

glossary_terms.definition: The transformation of English state finance in the 1690s through the creation of the Bank of England, the national debt, and a stock market, enabling the government to borrow large sums at low interest.
A joint-stock company chartered by Elizabeth I in 1600 to trade with Asia, which became the dominant force in Indian Ocean trade and later in Indian governance.
Present-day Kolkata in India; an East India Company trading post established in 1698 that became the centre of British trade with Bengal.
Companies owned collectively by shareholders who invest capital and share profits and losses, allowing large sums to be raised for risky ventures.
